results.derivation_summary: Section 1692e broadly bars a debt collector from using any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with collecting a debt, and then lists sixteen non-exhaustive examples of violations — including falsely claiming government affiliation or bonding (¶1), misstating the character, amount, or legal status of a debt or the collector's lawful fees (¶2), posing as an attorney (¶3), threatening arrest, seizure, garnishment, or other action that is unlawful or not actually intended (¶¶4–5), misrepresenting the effect of a transfer of the debt (¶6), imputing crime or disgraceful conduct (¶7), reporting known-false credit information or failing to note a debt is disputed (¶8), simulating court or government documents or misrepresenting documents as (or as not) legal process (¶¶9, 13, 15), using any false representation or deceptive means to collect or to obtain consumer information (¶10), failing to give the 'mini-Miranda' disclosures (¶11), falsely claiming accounts went to innocent purchasers for value (¶12), using a name other than the collector's true business name (¶14), and falsely implying the collector is or works for a consumer reporting agency under § 1681a(f) (¶16). The disclosure duty in ¶(11) is now implemented by Reg F, 12 C.F.R. § 1006.18(e), which requires the 'attempting to collect a debt / information will be used for that purpose' disclosure in the initial communication (repeated in the initial written communication if the first contact was oral), a 'this communication is from a debt collector' disclosure in all later communications, and exempts formal pleadings in a legal action. The section applies only to a 'debt collector' as defined in § 1692a(6) (subject to the § 1692a(6)(F) carve-outs, e.g., debts originated by the person or not in default when obtained) collecting a consumer 'debt' under § 1692a(5). edge_cases.scenario: A consumer brings in a collection letter from a debt buyer, received 20 months ago, that falsely stated a lawsuit had already been filed against her. She asks whether she has an FDCPA claim; the letter plainly matches catalog items (5) and (10).
edge_cases.gap_description: Neither the logic nor the checklist asks when the violation occurred relative to suit. 15 U.S.C. § 1692k(d) imposes a one-year limitations period running from the date of the violation (typically the date the letter was sent/received). The node would tell this consumer she has an independent § 1692e violation when her claim is already time-barred — a materially wrong practical answer. Ironically, the node asks about the state SOL on the underlying debt but never about the FDCPA's own SOL on the claim.

results.derivation_summary: Under 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a), unless the information is in the initial communication or the consumer has already paid, a debt collector must send a written notice within five days of the initial communication stating: (1) the amount of the debt; (2) the name of the creditor owed; (3) that the debt will be assumed valid unless the consumer disputes it within thirty days after receipt of the notice; (4) that a written dispute within the thirty-day period will cause the collector to obtain and mail verification of the debt or a copy of a judgment; and (5) that on written request within that period the collector will provide the name and address of the original creditor if different from the current creditor. Regulation F permits the validation information (12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(c)) to be given orally in the initial communication or by written notice in or within five days of that communication. edge_cases.scenario: A consumer was served with a credit-card collection complaint 45 days ago, panicked, and did nothing. No request for entry of default has been filed yet. He now asks what his deadline is and what he can do.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node encodes only the forward-looking 30-day computation and states that missing it means the plaintiff 'may apply for entry of default.' It has no branch for the very common posture of a defendant who is already past day 30. Under California practice an answer may still be filed and will be accepted at any time before default is actually entered (CCP § 585; clerk must reject a default request if an answer is on file), and after entry of default relief is available under CCP § 473(b) (six months, mistake/inadvertence/excusable neglect) or § 473(d)/473.5 for void judgments or lack of actual notice. As encoded, the rule reads as though the door has closed, which for a late-but-not-yet-defaulted debtor is affirmatively wrong and could cause them to abandon a case they could still defend.

edge_cases.scenario: A self-represented defendant, served personally on day 1, mails a handwritten answer to the clerk on day 28 with no filing fee and no fee-waiver application. The clerk returns it unfiled, and by the time she learns why, default has been requested.
edge_cases.gap_description: The rule tells the user only WHEN to file an answer and never that a first-appearance fee (roughly $225–$435 depending on limited/unlimited and amount, Gov. Code §§ 70611, 70613) must accompany it or that a fee waiver (form FW-001, Gov. Code § 68631) must be filed simultaneously. A timely-mailed but unfeed answer is rejected and does not stop default. edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer mails the summons, complaint, and a Notice and Acknowledgment of Receipt (form POS-015) to the defendant's home. The defendant reads the packet, never signs or returns the acknowledgment, and asks when her answer is due, counting from the postmark date.
edge_cases.gap_description: The service-completion note and checklist item 3 enumerate personal, substituted (§ 415.20), out-of-state mail (§ 415.40), and publication (§ 415.50) but omit in-state mail service by notice and acknowledgment under CCP § 415.30 — a routinely used, low-cost method in consumer debt cases. Under § 415.30(c), service is deemed complete on the date the defendant EXECUTES the acknowledgment; if it is never signed and returned, service is not effected at all and no answer clock ever starts (the plaintiff must serve another way and may recover the cost of further service). The encoded logic would start a 30-day clock from the mailing date, telling the defendant she is on a deadline — or already in default — when in fact she has not been served, and would also miss that the correct posture may be a § 418.10 motion to quash rather than an answer.

edge_cases.scenario: A tenant has a default judgment of possession entered against her in an eviction (forcible detainer) suit in justice court after she missed the hearing, and she asks two days later how to get it set aside.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's justice-court branch applies TRCP 505.3 (14 days to move to set aside, overruled at 21 days) to all justice court judgments, but eviction cases are governed by TRCP 510, which prevails over conflicting justice-court rules (TRCP 500.3(d)) and forecloses the motion-for-new-trial path in eviction cases; the operative remedy is a de novo appeal/appeal bond within 5 days of the judgment, after which a writ of possession can issue. Telling a defaulted tenant she has 14 days to file a motion to set aside is affirmatively wrong and will cause her to lose possession while the deadline that actually mattered runs. Default eviction judgments are among the most common Texas default judgments a lay user would present.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer concedes he was properly served with a debt-buyer suit but ignored it; a default judgment was signed and he learned of it about 45 days later. edge_cases.gap_description: The node makes the restricted-appeal (6-month) and bill-of-review alternatives available only in the 'defective/no service' branch. But a restricted appeal requires only that the party did not participate in the hearing, filed within 6 months, and that error is apparent on the face of the record -- defective service is merely the most common such error; unsupported unliquidated damages, a facially defective return of service, or a missing TRCP 239a certificate qualify equally. Because this person does not dispute service, the checklist's dispositive item 7 routes to 'no', the 30-day 329b window has closed, and the system would tell him no path remains -- materially wrong when a live restricted appeal exists. This posture (debt-buyer default with an inflated, unproven damages figure) is very common.

edge_cases.scenario: A defendant was validly served, defaulted, and the clerk never mailed the TRCP 306a notice of judgment; she first learned of the judgment when her bank account was frozen by a writ of garnishment roughly four months after the judgment was signed.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node correctly notes the TRCP 306a(4)-(5) restart caps at 90 days after signing, but it offers the bill of review only to defendants with a service defect. A defendant who was validly served yet received no notice of the judgment until after the 90-day cap can still pursue an equitable bill of review within four years (failure of official duty / no fault of her own), and may face a lower showing than the ordinary Baker v. Goldsmith elements. As encoded, the system would conclude both the 306a window and the service-defect exception are unavailable and imply the matter is closed, which is materially misleading. Learning of an old default judgment only via garnishment or wage withholding months later is a very common fact pattern.

Note the protection as written covers 'current wages for personal service'; the text does not address funds that are no longer current wages.

edge_cases.scenario: A family relocated from Illinois to Texas 14 months ago, bought a Houston home, and now wants to file Chapter 7 to discharge medical debt. They ask whether their Texas home is protected.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node addresses only the § 522(p) $214,000 cap on equity acquired in the 1,215-day window, but omits 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)'s 730-day domicile rule: a debtor domiciled in Texas for less than 730 days before filing cannot use Texas exemptions at all and must apply the exemptions of the state where they were domiciled for the greater part of the 180 days preceding that 730-day period (or federal exemptions if that state's are unavailable). For recent transplants — the very population the node flags — the answer is not 'uncapped, subject to a $214k cap' but 'you may get Illinois's much smaller homestead exemption or the federal $31,575 exemption.' That is a materially wrong answer for a common Texas fact pattern.

edge_cases.scenario: A contractor did a $70,000 remodel under a written contract signed only by the husband, with work beginning the day the contract was signed; he now files a mechanic's lien and threatens foreclosure. The wife asks whether the homestead is protected.
edge_cases.gap_description: The rule lists 'home-improvement liens contracted in writing' as a flat exception, and the checklist asks only whether the claim is such a lien. It omits the additional constitutional formalities of Tex. Const. art. XVI § 50(a)(5) — the contract must be signed by BOTH spouses, executed and filed with the county clerk BEFORE any material is furnished or labor performed, and (for a homestead) satisfy the five-day/three-day cooling-off and closing-location requirements. Defective execution is the single most common defense in homestead mechanic's-lien disputes; as encoded the node tells this homeowner the lien is enforceable when it is very likely void as to the homestead.

edge_cases.scenario: A homeowner with an old $40,000 abstract of judgment recorded in the county wants to sell her Austin homestead; the title company refuses to close unless the judgment is paid off, even though the property is clearly her homestead.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node says the homestead is exempt and that sale proceeds are protected for six months, which would tell this seller she has nothing to worry about. It omits that a recorded abstract of judgment creates a practical cloud on title that will block a sale, and the mechanism to clear it — the Tex. Prop. Code § 52.0012 homestead affidavit as release of judgment lien, with its notice-to-creditor and 30-day-objection procedure. The seller's actual problem is procedural clearance, and the encoded answer is materially misleading about her ability to close.

edge_cases.scenario: A judgment debtor with a family has $45,000 in a savings account, $20,000 of stock in a brokerage account, and a bass boat worth $12,000 — total well under $100,000 — and asks whether a judgment creditor can seize any of it. She reports no liens, no retirement accounts, and no jewelry/vehicle/firearm sub-limit problems.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node never enumerates the § 42.002(a) categories (home furnishings, food, clothing, tools/books of trade, two firearms, athletic/sporting equipment, vehicles, limited livestock and pets, etc.). It frames the analysis as 'aggregate FMV under the $100,000/$50,000 cap = exempt,' which invites the conclusion that ANY personal property under the cap is protected. In Texas, cash, bank deposits, brokerage/stock holdings, crypto, and recreational items like boats are simply not on the § 42.002(a) list and are 100% non-exempt regardless of value. A debtor told her under-cap property is exempt would get a flatly wrong and highly consequential answer. The checklist likewise asks only for 'aggregate fair market value of § 42.002(a)-listed property' without any item asking whether the targeted asset is on the list at all.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor who moved from Illinois to Texas 14 months ago is about to file Chapter 7 bankruptcy and asks how much of his personal property he can protect, listing household goods, a paid-off truck, and $200,000 in a rollover IRA.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node and checklist are silent on the bankruptcy context. Under 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A), a debtor domiciled in Texas for less than 730 days before filing must use the exemptions of his prior domicile (or the federal set), so the $100,000 family cap and the unlimited § 42.0021 retirement exemption may not be available at all; a Texas-eligible filer also has a federal-vs-state election that can change the outcome dramatically. Bankruptcy is one of the two dominant real-world postures in which Texas personal-property exemptions are asserted, and applying this node as encoded would give a recent transplant a materially wrong protection figure. No checklist item asks whether the matter is a bankruptcy case or how long the debtor has been domiciled in Texas.

edge_cases.scenario: A self-employed rideshare driver / 1099 consultant has a judgment against her. The creditor serves a writ of garnishment on the platform/client that owes her $8,000 in unpaid invoices, and she asks whether that money is protected as 'current wages.'
edge_cases.gap_description: The node states flatly that current wages are exempt in unlimited amount and that Texas 'separately prohibits wage garnishment outright for ordinary debts,' with the only qualification being the post-deposit/commingling note. Texas courts distinguish employee wages for personal services from independent-contractor accounts receivable, commissions, and draws, which are generally NOT protected 'current wages' and can be garnished in the obligor's hands. A gig/contract worker applying this node would be told her unpaid receivables are fully exempt when they are likely seizable. Neither the logic nor the checklist asks about the debtor's employment classification (W-2 employee vs. independent contractor/owner distributions).

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sues a consumer for $6,400 and files in a statutory county court at law (e.g., Harris County Civil Court at Law) rather than a justice court. The defendant, served by a private process server, checks the amount claimed ($6,400, under $20,000), concludes the justice-court node applies, and is told the answer is due 14 days after service.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist uses 'amount claimed ≤ $20,000' as a proxy for justice-court jurisdiction, but county and district courts have concurrent jurisdiction over sub-$20,000 debt claims and debt buyers routinely file there. In those courts the deadline is TRCP 99(b) (answer due by 10:00 a.m. on the Monday next after expiration of 20 days from service), not 14 days. The checklist never asks which court is named on the citation — the actually dispositive fact. A defendant on day 16 of a county-court suit would be told the deadline has passed and may abandon a timely defense.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer was served 25 days ago with a justice-court debt claim, panicked, did nothing, and now asks whether it is worth filing an answer. No default judgment has been entered yet and the plaintiff has not requested one.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node presents the 14-day date as a hard cutoff with no treatment of the post-deadline posture. Under Texas practice a default judgment cannot be entered while an answer is on file, so a late answer filed before default is effective and is the single most consequential piece of advice for the very common 'I already missed it' fact pattern. As encoded, the rule materially misleads such a person into inaction and a default judgment that was avoidable.

edge_cases.scenario: A justice court clerk serves the citation and petition by certified mail rather than by constable; the defendant signs the return receipt on a Wednesday, three days after the clerk mailed it, and asks when the answer is due.
